[[File:Gold medal of Toni Merkens, 1936 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|A gold medal from the 1936 Olympics|alt=A tarnished gold medal featuring a person in a toga, and the words "XI Olympiade Berlin 1936".]]
{{1936 Summer Olympics}}

The [[1936 Summer Olympics]], officially known as the Games of the XI Olympiad, was an international [[multi-sport event]] held in [[Berlin]], [[Nazi Germany|Germany]], from 1 August to 16 August.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|last=Johnston|first=Mindy|title=Berlin 1936 Olympic Games|url=https://www.britannica.com/event/Berlin-1936-Olympic-Games|encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]|date=25 July 2024|access-date=13 September 2024|archive-date=May 15, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190515161823/https://www.britannica.com/event/Berlin-1936-Olympic-Games|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Berlin had previously been chosen to host the [[1916 Summer Olympics]], which were subsequently cancelled due to the [[First World War]].<ref name=eurosportberlin1936>{{cite news|title=Olympic history: Berlin 1936|url=http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/blogs/world-of-sport/olympic-countdown-berlin-1936-132812934.html|access-date=March 15, 2012|newspaper=Eurosport|date=March 12, 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316093719/http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/blogs/world-of-sport/olympic-countdown-berlin-1936-132812934.html|archive-date=March 16, 2012|df=mdy-all}}</ref> The 1936 Games had 3,963 athletes from 49 [[National Olympic Committee]]s (NOCs) participating in a total of 129 events in 19 sports. This was the highest number of nations represented at any Games to date.<ref name=holocaustmuseumboycott/> Athletes from 32 NOCs won medals, of which 21 secured at least one gold medal, and 17 NOCs won no medals. The host NOC, [[Germany at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Germany]], received a total of 101 medals (38 of them gold),<ref name=MedalTable/> the most of any nation and a record for a united German team, although [[East Germany at the Olympics|East Germany]] broke that record in [[East Germany at the 1976 Summer Olympics|1976]], [[East Germany at the 1980 Summer Olympics|1980]] and [[East Germany at the 1988 Summer Olympics|1988]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Olympic Medal Table|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/olympics/8660580/Olympic-Medal-Table.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727194619/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/olympics/8660580/Olympic-Medal-Table.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 27, 2011|access-date=March 28, 2012|newspaper=The Daily Telegraph}}</ref>

A boycott by the United States was suggested due to Germany's [[Nazi Germany|Nazi regime]], but it was not implemented.<ref name=eurosportberlin1936 /> The other NOCs which threatened to boycott the Games for the same reason were the United Kingdom, France, Sweden, Czechoslovakia and the Netherlands.<ref name=holocaustmuseumboycott>{{cite web|title=The Movement to Boycott the Berlin Olympics of 1936|url=http://www.ushmm.org/wlc/en/article.php?ModuleId=10007087|publisher=United States Holocaust Memorial Museum|access-date=March 17, 2012|archive-date=February 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160220064137/http://www.ushmm.org/wlc/en/article.php?ModuleId=10007087|url-status=live}}</ref> An alternative [[People's Olympiad]] was planned to take place in [[Barcelona]], Spain, but was cancelled at the last moment following the outbreak of the [[Spanish Civil War]] after the athletes had already begun to arrive.<ref name=holocaustmuseumboycott/> The civil war also meant that Spain's NOC did not compete at the 1936 Games.<ref name=eurosportberlin1936 /> While no NOCs ended up boycotting the Games on anti-Nazi grounds, a multinational Jewish-led boycott of the Games took place, with an individual athlete refusing to take part.<ref>{{cite news|last=Pope|first=John|title=Fred Feran, who boycotted 1936 Olympics in Berlin, dies at age 92|url=http://www.nola.com/news/index.ssf/2010/03/fred_feran_who_boycotted_1936.html|access-date=March 17, 2012|newspaper=New Orleans Metro|date=1 March 2010|archive-date=September 7, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120907011759/http://www.nola.com/news/index.ssf/2010/03/fred_feran_who_boycotted_1936.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Also, the [[IAAF]]s' refusal to allow athletes from [[Northern Ireland]] to compete for the [[Irish Olympic Council]] in [[Athletics at the 1936 Summer Olympics|athletics events]] led the [[Irish Free State]] to boycott.<ref name="sullivan">{{cite journal |last=O'Sullivan |first=Patrick T. |date=Spring 1998 |title=Ireland & the Olympic Games |journal=History Ireland |location=Dublin |volume=6 |issue=1 |url=http://www.historyireland.com/volumes/volume6/issue1/features/?id=180 |access-date=August 1, 2016 |archive-date=December 16, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121216072750/http://www.historyireland.com/volumes/volume6/issue1/features/?id=180 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Krüger|first=Arnd |author2=William J. Murray|title=The Nazi Olympics: sport, politics and appeasement in the 1930s |publisher=University of Illinois Press|year=2003 |page=230 |isbn=0-252-02815-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s5ntIQv0W5IC&q=1936+olympics+%22irish+free+state%22&pg=PA230 }}</ref>

[[Marjorie Gestring]] became the youngest Olympic champion ever at the age of 13,{{#tag:ref|In the [[Rowing at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Men's coxed pair|1900 men's coxed pair rowing]], an unidentified boy aged 12 or less coxed the winning pair in the final; however, only semifinal cox [[Hermanus Brockmann]] is listed by the IOC.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.olympic.org/hermanus-gerardus-brockmann|title=Hermanus Gerardus BROCKMANN — Olympic Rowing|work=[[International Olympic Committee]]|access-date=2 August 2016|archive-date=August 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160815105059/https://www.olympic.org/hermanus-gerardus-brockmann|url-status=live}}</ref> Winners received silver medals at the [[1900 Summer Olympics|1900 games]].<ref name="Mallon">{{cite book | author = Mallon, Bill | year = 1998 | title = The 1900 Olympic Games, Results for All Competitors in All Events, with Commentary | publisher = McFarland & Company, Inc., Publishers | location = Jefferson, North Carolina | isbn = 0-7864-0378-0 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/1900olympicgames00mall }}</ref>|group="nb"|name="brockmann"}} winning a gold medal in the [[Diving at the 1936 Summer Olympics – Women's 3 metre springboard|women's 3 meter springboard]].<ref name=eurosportberlin1936 /> As [[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea was under Japanese rule]], Korean athletes who hoped to compete in the Games were required to qualify for the [[Japan at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Japanese team]]. [[Sohn Kee-chung]], competing as Kitei Son, won gold in the [[Athletics at the 1936 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon|marathon]], which made him Japan's first gold medalist at these Games and the first Korean ever to win a medal.<ref name=kitei>{{cite web|title=Kitei Son|url=http://www.olympic.org/kitei-son|publisher=Olympic.org|access-date=March 17, 2012|archive-date=August 24, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120824055733/http://www.olympic.org/kitei-son|url-status=live}}</ref> His fellow countryman [[Nam Sung-yong]] won the bronze medal in the same event.<ref name=obitsohnguardian>{{cite news|last=Lewis|first=Mike|title=Obituary: Sohn Kee-chung|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2002/nov/30/guardianobituaries|access-date=March 17, 2012|newspaper=The Guardian|date=30 November 2002}}</ref><ref name=eurosportberlin1936 />

==Medal table==
[[File:Ibolya Csak.jpg|thumb|right|upright|[[Ibolya Csák]], gold medallist for Hungary in the [[Athletics at the 1936 Summer Olympics – Women's high jump|women's high jump]]|alt=A black and white photograph of a female athlete with short cut hair. She wears a white sleeveless top with two horizontal stripes and a crest in the middle of her chest, and dark shorts.]]
[[File:Berlin, Olympiade, Tilly Fleischer.jpg|thumb|right|upright|[[Tilly Fleischer]], gold medallist for Germany in the [[Athletics at the 1936 Summer Olympics – Women's javelin throw|women's javelin]]|alt=A black and white photograph of a female athlete in an all-white outfit with the Nazi eagle and swastika in the middle of her chest. She holds a small plant and wears an laurel wreath on her head.]]
The medal table is based on information provided by the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) and is consistent with IOC convention in its published medal tables. The table uses the [[Olympic medal table]] sorting method. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won, where 'nation' is an entity represented by a [[National Olympic Committee]] (NOC). The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next, and then the number of bronze medals.<ref>{{cite news |title=Olympic medal table: USA beat China to top spot at Paris 2024 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2580716.html |work=[[The Independent]] | date=11 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240812015233/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2594580.html |archive-date=12 August 2024 |url-status=live |last1=Ostlere |first1=Lawrence |access-date=12 August 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=A Medal Count That Adds Up To Little |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |work=[[The New York Times]] | date=18 August 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321004238/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |archive-date=21 March 2023 |url-status=live |last1=Araton |first1=Harvey |url-access=subscription |access-date=25 July 2024 }}</ref> If teams are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by their [[List of IOC country codes|IOC country code]].<ref>{{cite news |title=What happens if two countries are tied in the Olympic medal table? Tiebreaker rules explained |url=https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |work=[[Diario AS]] |date=10 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811152350/https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |archive-date=August 11, 2024 |url-status=live |last1=Cons |first1=Roddy |access-date=11 August 2024 |language=en-us }}</ref>

A dead heat in the lightweight section of the [[Weightlifting at the 1936 Summer Olympics|weightlifting]] competition resulted in gold medals being awarded to both [[Austria at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Austria]]'s [[Robert Fein]] and [[Egypt at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Egypt]]'s Anwar Mesbah, and resulted in a silver medal not being awarded for that event. A dead heat for third place in the floor competition of the [[Gymnastics at the 1936 Summer Olympics|gymnastic]] events resulted in bronze medals going to both [[Germany at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Germany]]'s [[Konrad Frey]] and [[Eugen Mack]] of [[Switzerland at the 1936 Summer Olympics|Switzerland]]. This resulted in 130 gold and bronze medals being awarded, but only 128 silver medals.<ref name="official report">{{cite web|title=The Official Report of the Organising Committee for the XI Olympiad |url=http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1936/1936v2sum.pdf |publisher=The Organising Committee for the XI Olympiad |year=1936 |volume=II |access-date=March 17, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080406153656/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1936/1936v2sum.pdf |archive-date=April 6, 2008 }}</ref>
